description: We're a chill team looking to build cool stuff, share ideas, and learn along the way. Open to collaborating with people who are passionate, creative, and ready to contribute. All skills and ideas are welcome!
summary:
Earth System Trend Detective is a web tool that turns students into data detectives. You ask a question in plain words, such as “Is rainfall changing in Chennai since 2001?” The tool fetches official NASA and NOAA data (Giovanni, MERRA-2, AppEEARS, Cloud OPeNDAP, ERDDAP), builds a monthly time series, and tests whether the trend is real.

Beyond a single number, it checks whether the conclusion can be trusted. It flags possible instrument effects at satellite changeovers. A “Trend Court” of statistical tests reaches a verdict. BEAST and PELT find when change began, and the tool estimates how many more years of data a weak trend needs. It also compares the real data with random shuffles to ask “could it be chance?”

A DigiTwin mode simulates what-if scenarios for several places at once, always labelled “simulated, not a prediction.” A local Qwen language model explains every result in simple language, with its numbers checked against the analysis. AirLLM lets students run it on low-spec laptops.

Climate claims spread faster than evidence. Our tool teaches the next generation to tell real trends from noise, honestly and reproducibly.
details:
What it does: Earth System Trend Detective helps students check whether an Earth trend is real. A student types a question in plain language, for example “Is rainfall changing in Chennai since 2001?” The tool finds the right dataset and fetches official NASA and NOAA data, from Giovanni/MERRA-2, Harmony, Cloud OPeNDAP, AppEEARS and NOAA ERDDAP. It then builds a monthly time series and tests the trend.

How it works:

  • Integrity check: flags gaps and possible instrument effects where satellites change.
  • Trend Court: several statistical tests (Mann-Kendall, Sen’s slope, regression with autocorrelation correction) reach one verdict: SIGNIFICANT or NOT PROVEN.
  • Change points: BEAST and PELT estimate when a change began.
  • Evidence Clock: shows how many more years of data a weak trend needs.
  • Could it be chance?: compares the real data with random shuffles of the same data.
  • DigiTwin: simulates what-if scenarios (e.g. +2 °C) for several places side by side. Results are clearly labelled “simulated, not a prediction.”
  • Paper replication: reproduces a published SeaWiFS study.
  • Plain-language explanations: a local Qwen language model (Ollama) writes them, and every number it uses is checked against the analysis. AirLLM lets students with low-spec laptops run larger models.

Benefits and impact: students learn to tell real trends from noise and to state results honestly (“consistent with”, not “caused by”). Every chart shows its data source, version and DOI, so results can be reproduced.

Tools: Python (FastAPI, NumPy, pandas, xarray, statsmodels, Rbeast), React with TypeScript (Vite), Plotly and Three.js, Ollama with Qwen, AirLLM. AI tools (Claude) helped with coding, debugging, research and writing, and that is acknowledged in our repository.

What makes it creative: instead of only showing a trend line, it puts each trend “on trial” and shows how strong the evidence is.

Factors we considered: scientific honesty, student-friendly language, reproducibility, and running on ordinary laptops.
